paper_title: Vision-Language-Action or World-Action? Just Action Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: The vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action model (WAM) communities debate whether control policies should inherit pretrained knowledge from vision-language models or from visual generators. The debate, however, bundles three separable choices: backbone initialization, the objective applied to future observations, and whether the machinery for that future loss is kept at inference. A gap between a VLA and a WAM therefore cannot simply be attributed to any one of them. We show that decoupling these choices yields a common framework for both families, which we term Just Action Model (JAM): a pretrained visual backbone with an action expert, trained with an action loss and a foresight loss. The foresight loss trains current-observation features to predict frozen encodings of the recorded future through a prediction head discarded after training, so no visual generation is involved in either training or inference, and the backbone can be chosen freely. We first compare objectives within fixed policy architectures, then evaluate the foresight recipe across backbone families. The resulting JAM policies outperform their matched FastWAM and ImageWAM counterparts on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, and achieve similar or slightly higher success rates on RoboTwin. Compared with FastWAM, JAM improves the success rates from 97.0%/55.3%/91.2% to 98.2%/64.5%/91.4%, respectively. With cached foresight targets, JAM reduces estimated online training FLOPs per sample per update by 73% relative to FastWAM. Our results show that future supervision improves control without visual generation or additional inference machinery, and strong foresight performance is attainable with either generator-initialized or vision-language backbones. sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Pretrained visual models provide starting point for robot control. Standard vision-languageaction models (VLAs) adapt vision-language representations to predict actions (Kim et al., 2025b; Black et al., 2025a;b). World-action models (WAMs) start from image or video generators and learn actions together with future visual prediction (Ye et al., 2026b; Yuan et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026b; Bi et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a). These approaches differ, as depicted in Figure 1, in both their pretrained knowledge and how they use the robot trajectories: most VLAs learn only the actions in trajectory, whereas WAM also learns to generate the observations that follow. Comparing their success rates alone does not identify which difference matters. We separate three choices: backbone initialization, the objective on recorded future observations, and the modules used at inference. Recent attempts such as FastWAM (Yuan et al., 2026) and ImageWAM (Zhang et al., 2026a) remove test-time video or image generation and suggest that visual generative objectives at training time are the key to WAMs. We ask more basic question: does Corresponding author. 1 Figure 1: The three choices that separate VLAs, WAMs, and JAM: backbone initialization, the objective on recorded future observations, and the modules kept at inference. (a) The VLA reference uses no future objective, only the action loss Lact. (b) WAMs add visual generation loss LG. The dashed loop shows generated future observations entering the action expert in some WAMs. (c) JAM uses foresight loss LF across pretraining families, discards its supervision branch, and retains the corresponding action path. learning from recorded future observations require visual generative objective at all? If not, can backbones without visual generative pretraining learn from future observations in the same way? We show that predicting future representations can replace visual generative supervision in policy training. We introduce Just Action Model (JAM), common recipe for pretrained visual backbone and an action expert. The policy is trained with an action loss and foresight loss: prediction head maps current-observation features to targets supplied by frozen future anchor. Future observations provide targets for the foresight loss, never inputs to the action path. The anchor branch and prediction head are used only during training, and fixed targets can be cached. At deployment, the backbone encodes the current context and the action expert predicts the action chunk. JAM requires no image or video generation during policy fine-tuning or deployment. The backbone may still come from generative pretraining, and the action expert still uses flow matching. We evaluate the recipe in two stages. First, we replace the generative objectives of FastWAM and ImageWAM while keeping each policys architecture, data, optimizer, training budget, and deployment path fixed. Predicting future representations preserves or improves success, and targets at future positions are more effective than those at the current position. Backbone and future anchor pretraining play different roles: pretrained FastWAM backbone remains effective with randomly initialized, frozen future anchor, and direct VAE features give its strongest result. JAM (Ovis-U1) performs best with targets from the pretrained Yak backbone, so the preferred target is architecturedependent. With the best target for each architecture, LIBERO-Plus success rises from 55.31% to 64.54% for FastWAM and from 65.27% to 79.95% for ImageWAM. With cached targets, this recipe reduces estimated online FLOPs per sample per update by 73.0% for FastWAM and 36.8% for ImageWAM. Second, we retain the common foresight objective and instantiate it with generative, self-supervised, and vision-language backbones. On LIBERO-Plus, JAM (Ovis-U1), JAM (DINOv2-L), and JAM (Qwen3.5-2B) reach 79.95%, 70.39%, and 81.14%, against 65.27% for ImageWAM (Ovis-U1), which is trained with the generation loss LG. These results establish the recipes applicability across all three families: generative backbones can learn from future observations without visual generative loss, and the same supervision applies to non-generative backbones. Our contributions are: We propose JAM, single recipe for pretrained visual backbone and an action expert in which recorded future observations enter only as frozen prediction targets, and the foresight branch is discarded after training. We show through fixed-architecture comparisons that foresight can replace visual generation while preserving or improving success. Future-offset targets are more effective than current-offset targets, and the best target depends on the backbone: plain VAE suffices for 2 the Wan video backbone. With targets cached, JAM reduces the estimated online training FLOPs per sample per update by 73.0% relative to FastWAM. We apply the same objective to generative, self-supervised, and vision-language backbones, with the strongest generative and vision-language instantiations achieving comparable control performance, showing that strong performance with foresight is attainable using either generator-initialized or vision-language backbone.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Pretrained models for robot control. OpenVLA adapts vision-language model to autoregressive action prediction; π0 and π0.5 pair vision-language backbones with flow-matching action experts (Kim et al., 2025b; Black et al., 2025a;b). WAMs combine generator initialization with future visual prediction (Ye et al., 2026a;b; Li et al., 2026b; Bi et al., 2026). FastWAM retains video co-training without test-time video generation (Yuan et al., 2026); ImageWAM uses an image-editing backbone and future-image target (Zhang et al., 2026a). JAM replaces their visual generation objectives while preserving each policys architecture and deployment path, separating the use of pretrained generators from the need to generate during policy training. Future-representation supervision. Future observations support planning and predictive supervision (Wu et al., 2024; Cheang et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025). Joint-embedding methods avoid pixel reconstruction (Assran et al., 2025; Daithankar et al., 2026); Var-JEPA studies variational formulation on tabular data (Gogl & Yau, 2026). Mirai and Video-Mirai apply foresight to image and video generation (Yu et al., 2026b;a). For control, FRAPPE aligns policy features with multiple future representations, VLAFlow pairs latent alignment with languagesupervised co-training, and Being-H0.7 aligns deployable prior with future-informed posterior (Zhao et al., 2026; Xia et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2026). VLA-JEPA uses frozen video targets for human-video pretraining and joint representation and action learning (Sun et al., 2026); PFD distills future-conditioned action residuals into current-only FastWAM policy while retaining video co-training and deployed residual adapter (Fang et al., 2026). Predictive supervision for action policies. FLARE mixes future, state, and action tokens through JEPA-WAM supervises shared actionself-attention in the action DiT (Zheng et al., 2025). generating predictor using dense joint currentfuture targets in frozen V-JEPA space. Its pretrained-VLA instantiation preserves the original pathways and removes the prediction branch at deployment (Lin et al., 2026). JAM differs from FLARE in where prediction is applied: separate training-only head supervises existing visual-backbone tokens, preserving the matched policys action computation. In contrast to JEPA-WAMs joint currentfuture V-JEPA target, it supervises future-position features in target space chosen for each backbone. This common recipe replaces visual generation in existing WAMs and extends across generative, self-supervised, and vision-language backbones. Appendix gives further comparisons and more related work. 3 JAM: JUST ACTION MODELS

sections.title: INSTANTIATIONS ACROSS PRETRAINING FAMILIES
sections.content: We instantiate JAM with backbones from three pretraining families. In the cross-backbone comparison in Table 3, each future anchor is frozen copy of the corresponding backbone. Our matched FastWAM and ImageWAM experiments additionally evaluate VAE-direct future anchors. Generative backbones. FastWAM pairs Wan2.2-5B video backbone with an action expert of the same depth, and ImageWAM (Ovis-U1) pairs the pretrained Yak18 image-editing backbone with an 18-block action expert of matching width (Team Wan et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a). Their generative objectives denoise future video latents and generate future image. Under JAM, the backbone sees only the clean current frame, and the policy architecture and action-expert initialization are unchanged. Two further targets isolate what the frozen generator contributes: the same backbone with random initialization, which keeps the architecture but removes the pretrained features, and the frozen VAE tokenizer alone, which removes the target transformer and predicts lifted latent-patch features. Self-supervised backbones. DINOv2 is an image encoder with no language input and no generative head (Oquab et al., 2024). The action expert mirrors the backbones transformer blocks, and separate text encoder supplies instruction features to the action expert, but not to the visual backbone. Vision-language backbone. Qwen3.5-2B is vision-language model that already reads images and text together (Qwen Team, 2026). The action expert mirrors the backbones blocks and reads the backbones tokens through causal token mixing over image, text, and action tokens, so it is VLA trained with an additional foresight loss.

sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: Our study has two stages. First, we replace visual generation with foresight within fixed policy architectures and deployment paths, examining target offsets and future anchors. Second, we apply the common objective to backbones from different pretraining families. We also compare the resulting policies with published systems and evaluate training cost.

sections.title: 4.3 VARYING THE BACKBONE
sections.content: Having replaced visual generation with foresight and compared different target representations, we next examine the role of backbone pretraining and whether the same recipe extends beyond generative backbones. Table 2 separates backbone and future anchor initialization for JAM (Wan). With pretrained visual backbone, pretrained and random Wan targets reach 97.45% and 97.65% on LIBERO. With random visual backbone, they reach 71.15% and 84.40%. Pretrained backbone weights are important in both matched-target comparisons, whereas random target remains effective. frozen random future anchor supplies stable, input-dependent features of the recorded future, not independently sampled noise. Together with the VAE results in Table 1, this shows that the future anchor need not use the same pretrained backbone as the policy, while the policy backbone still relies on pretraining for strong control performance. sections.title: 4.5 TRAINING COST
sections.content: JAM reduces online training cost by processing only the current observation in the trainable visual branch and caching fixed targets. With cached foresight targets, the estimated cost per sample per update falls from 15.52 TFLOPs for FastWAM to 4.19 for JAM (Wan), 73.0% reduction. Generation denoises nine-frame window that the video VAE must also encode, whereas cached foresight uses only the current frame online. With cached Yak targets, the estimated cost falls from 5.81 TFLOPs for ImageWAM (Ovis-U1) to 3.67 for JAM (Ovis-U1), 36.8% reduction. Its generative branch predicts only one future frame, and both objectives process the text context. Measured on one GH200, the GPU time of the operations covered by these estimates falls by 67.3% and 37.8% in the same two comparisons. Appendix details the FLOP estimates and GPU-time measurements.

sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: JAM bridges vision-language-action and world-action models by separating backbone initialization, supervision on future observations, and the modules retained at inference. It trains pretrained visual backbone and an action expert with action and foresight losses, using frozen future representations as targets and discarding the foresight branch after training. With the policy architecture fixed, replacing visual generation with foresight yields higher success rates than the corresponding gener9 ative baselines on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, with the largest gains on LIBERO-Plus; RoboTwin 2.0 success is similar or slightly higher. With cached targets, JAM reduces online FLOPs per sample per update by 73.0% relative to FastWAM and 36.8% relative to ImageWAM. With the recipe fixed, the same supervision applies to generative, self-supervised, and vision-language backbones, and the best generator-initialized and vision-language policies achieve comparable performance. These results show that effective foresight training is possible with either pretraining family, while the cross-backbone comparison does not isolate the effect of pretraining alone. Both families can be trained as Just Action Models that learn from recorded futures without visual generation during policy training or additional inference machinery.

sections.title: ETHICS STATEMENT
sections.content: This study evaluates robot manipulation policies in simulation using public models, code, and datasets. Experiments use LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin 2.0 and involve no human participants or personal data. Relevant risks include failures under distribution shift and unsafe deployment of simulation-trained policies without physical validation.

sections.title: A IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS
sections.content: A.1 TRAINING SETUP All runs use eight NVIDIA GH200 GPUs and bf16 mixed precision. We use AdamW with betas (0.9, 0.95) and weight decay 0.01, learning rate of 104 with cosine decay and 5% warmup, and gradient clipping at 1.0. With Wan, JAM follows the FastWAM recipe: ZeRO-1, 32-step action chunks, and targets from recorded future window. Ovis-U1, FLUX.2, Qwen3.5-2B, and DINOv2-B/L follow the ImageWAM recipe: ZeRO-0, 16-step action chunks, and targets from the recorded endpoint. Future observations enter only the future-anchor branch. LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus. Both recipes use two 224224 camera views and global batch size 128. FastWAM trains for 20k updates and ImageWAM for 21.7k. RoboTwin 2.0. All policies use the same three camera views. FastWAM combines them into 384320 image, and Ovis-U1 and FLUX.2 into 288256 image. Qwen3.5-2B encodes the three views separately at 224224 per view. All policies are trained for five epochs. FastWAM uses global batch size 1,024 and 29,355 updates; the ImageWAM recipe uses global batch size 384 and 69,900 updates. A.2 BACKBONES AND TARGET INTERFACES Table 7 summarizes the training targets and action contexts for each backbone. Wan. FastWAM pairs 30-block Wan2.2-5B backbone with matching action expert through directional mixed attention (Team Wan et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2026). The two LIBERO views form 224448 frame with 98 current-frame latent tokens. The nine-frame target window becomes three temporal VAE positions; readouts [1, 2] span steps 416 and 2032. Alignment uses fixed spatial indices without object tracking. VAE-direct targets lift each 2248 patch from 192 to 3,072 dimensions by fixed coordinate repetition and scaling, preserving norms and cosine similarities. The frozen Wan future anchors in Table 1 use pretrained weights or default random initialization. The EMA future anchor in Table 10 uses an FP32 copy of the policy backbone updated with decay 0.995. For the readout ablation, the pretrained Wan future anchor receives the same full clean window at diffusion time = 0. We align policy predictions to its current-position features at [0], future-position features at [1, 2], or both at [0, 1, 2]. Bidirectional attention can encode future context implicitly at [0]. Future-only supervision explicitly targets the future positions at [1, 2]. Ovis-U1. We retain ImageWAMs Yak18 backbone, with six double-stream and twelve singlestream blocks at width 1,536, and its matching action expert (Zhang et al., 2026a). The expert attends to text, condition-image, and action keys. Two LIBERO views form 224448 frame with 1428 packed Ovis-VAE tokens; frozen Ovis stack supplies text features. The frozen Yak future anchor reads the current frame, text, and 16-step future frame; target tokens are excluded from the trainable stream. Random-Yak and VAE-direct controls keep readouts and training budgets fixed. VAE-direct lifts 16-dimensional tokens to 1,536 dimensions using Wans norm-preserving map, without target transformer or text conditioning. FLUX.2. We use ImageWAMs FLUX.2 Klein 4B backbone with five double-stream and twenty single-stream blocks, paired with matching action expert of width 1,024. Instructions are 512 cached tokens from frozen Qwen3-4B text encoder. The frozen FLUX.2 future anchor reads the current frame, instruction features, and 16-step future frame at diffusion time = 0. Qwen3.5-2B. The 24-layer backbone encodes each view separately alongside the instruction, without separate text encoder. Its action expert copies compatible weights from 18 GatedDeltaNet and six full-attention blocks and adds action input, output, and flow-time modules. Causal token mixers process the current imagetext prefix before action tokens, preventing actions from influencing the prefix. The frozen future anchor reads the instruction, current views, and 16-step future views in one causal sequence. Future-image features supervise current-image features at the same layer; future views never enter the policy prefix. DINOv2-B/L. Each encoder processes views separately. Its action expert matches its depth and width, copies normalization, attention, and MLP weights, and adds action input, position, flowtime, AdaLN, and output modules. Action queries attend to the text prefix, same-layer patch keys and values from both views, and action tokens; visual queries never attend to text or actions. The text prefix contains 512 cached tokens from frozen Qwen3-4B, projected to the action width. frozen DINOv2 copy encodes each future view into final-layer patch targets for the corresponding policy layer. sections.title: E EXTENDED RELATED WORK
sections.content: Video-based policies and joint visualaction models combine action learning with visual prediction (Wu et al., 2024; Cheang et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025). VPP and Seer connect predictive visual features to control (Hu et al., 2025; Tian et al., 2025). Other policies use generated observations or predictive latent context during action selection (Zhang et al., 2026b; Li et al., 2026a; Wang et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026). Action-conditioned latent prediction. V-JEPA 2-AC trains an action-conditioned predictor on robot trajectories using frozen video features, then uses latent rollouts for model-predictive control toward an image goal (Assran et al., 2025). JAM uses future targets to learn policy representations for imitation learning. It discards the prediction head after training and samples actions without latent rollouts or planning. Predictive representations in action policies. FLARE mixes future, state, and action tokens in the action DiT (Zheng et al., 2025). FRAPPE retains multiple prefix-and-LoRA streams at inference (Zhao et al., 2026). VLAFlows MindWPI adds current-observation V-JEPA context accessible to action tokens (Xia et al., 2026). JAM supervises existing visual-backbone tokens through separate training-only head, preserving the matched baselines action computation. Representations and visual generation. REPA aligns diffusion features with visual representations, AGRA adds semantic alignment to WAM co-training, and Video-Mirai adds foresight to autoregressive video diffusion; all retain visual generation (Yu et al., 2025; Qiu et al., 2026; Yu et al., 2026a). WAM4D adds structured visual supervision to world-action learning (Li et al., 2026c). JAM removes visual generation during policy fine-tuning and uses no predicted future features as action inputs. Frozen and adaptive targets. Frozen random encoders map input to targets (Burda et al., 2019; Sarnthein et al., 2023). Noise As Targets learns assignments to fixed random vectors (Bojanowski & Joulin, 2017). EMA encoders update their weights during training (Grill et al., 2020).
